transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Avery Chen; Marco Alvarez; Priya Singh (Redwood) — Lena Morris; Doug Patel; Rachel Kim; Sam O'Donnell (Beacon)

[00:00] Avery Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off in a sec, uh lena, sam, can you hear me ok?
[00:06] Lena Morris: yeah, good to go, thanks a lot.
[00:09] Avery Chen: cool. quick agenda — compare dedicated/reserved capacity versus hosted routing for latency slas, dig into noisy neighbor mitigations, kv cache sizing, batching windows, quantization impacts, and vpc/on-prem notes. sound good?
[00:23] Doug Patel: yep, all that plus we want to validate throughput guarantees because we have peaks at end of month.
[00:28] Marco Alvarez: great, i'll start with a sketch of the runtime behaviors. right now our serving runtime does continuous batching with dynamic batch windows — so for small interactive calls we try to keep batch latencies under 30ms additional, but as you scale up that window can hit 100-200ms if you prioritize throughput.
[00:46] Sam O'Donnell: can you clarify 'continuous batching'? how is that different from batching at ingress?
[00:51] Marco Alvarez: yeah, good question. so continuous batching is intra-GPU kernel coalescing — we keep small queues and aggregate tokens across concurrent requests rather than waiting on a hard timer only. it reduces per-token compute overhead but it can increase tail latency if concurrency patterns are bursty.
[01:10] Lena Morris: are there knobs to tune that per-route? like for our chat assistant we need tight p95 under 250ms, but for summarization we can tolerate higher latency.
[01:19] Priya Singh: absolutely — routing policies let you set per-route target latency buckets and priority. on Dedicated you can then map those to isolated pools with guaranteed throughput and hard CPU/GPU quotas.
[01:27] Rachel Kim: on security, if we go Dedicated, do audit logs and kms integrate with our enterprise KMS?
[01:33] Avery Chen: yes — Dedicated and Private support customer-managed KMS, and audit logs are shipped to your SIEM over secure channels. we'll send the SOC2/ISO packet after this call.
[01:41] Doug Patel: back to noisy neighbor — what's the playbook? we've hit situations historically where one tenant's long generations spiked GPU memory and slowed everyone else.
[01:50] Marco Alvarez: we use a mix: tenant fencing for Dedicated, runtime soft-limits, and eviction policies for the KV cache. specifically, Dedicated pools can be single-tenant GPUs or single-tenant pods depending on the card. in hosted multi-tenant, we do aggressive token throttles and automatic fallbacks to smaller model variants when contention detected.
[02:10] Sam O'Donnell: how detectable is that contention? is it reactive after latency increases or do you predict it?
[02:15] Marco Alvarez: both. telemetry picks up queue length and GPU utilization. we have a moving-window anomaly detector — when it crosses thresholds we either throttle or shift routing to a dedicated reserve or fallback model. in Dedicated you avoid multi-tenant noisy neighbor by design.
[02:28] Lena Morris: what's the expected p95/p99 delta between Hosted and Dedicated for our workload?
[02:34] Marco Alvarez: from similar healthcare customers, Hosted p95 is often 1.2–1.5x Dedicated p95 under heavy load; p99 can be worse if there's KV thrashing. for example, a 32k-context summarization job saw p95 320ms Dedicated vs 450ms Hosted in our last test, but again that's workload-dependent.
[02:52] Doug Patel: you mentioned KV thrashing — let's dive into the KV cache sizing.
[02:56] Marco Alvarez: sure. KV cache is our prefix/cached keys for autoregressive decoders. sizing depends on concurrency and typical seq len. we recommend capacity planning: keep hot-set of keys for top 10% of requests, ttl-based eviction for older sessions, and prefetching for long context scenarios. prefetch can add some CPU overhead but reduces p99 significantly.
[03:18] Sam O'Donnell: prefetch—isn't that risky? it might load the cache with irrelevant keys and push out other hot keys.
[03:24] Priya Singh: true — that's why we have an LRU with weighted heuristics: weight by recent access frequency and model seq length. we can tune TTLs per-customer and route. we also support shard-aware eviction so high-throughput tenants don't evict less-active but critical sessions.
[03:40] Lena Morris: do you have numbers for p99 improvement with prefetch?
[03:44] Marco Alvarez: ballpark: enabling targeted prefetch for long-session workflows reduced p99 by 25–40% in our internal sims; it added about 5–8% memory pressure on GPU, so it's a tradeoff.
[03:55] Rachel Kim: memory pressure concerns us — on Dedicated we can choose instance types with more GPU memory, right?
[03:59] Priya Singh: yes, Dedicated lets you pick larger GPU SKUs and reserve more KV memory. you can also enable strict eviction policies and per-tenant cache caps.
[04:07] Doug Patel: quantization — will q4/q8 give us gains on latency and do we risk degraded output quality for our medical summaries?
[04:14] Marco Alvarez: quantization does reduce memory bandwidth and can speed up kernels a bit, but the real latency wins come from smaller memory footprints enabling bigger caches and better batching. quality impact depends on model and quantization scheme — our recommendation is to run an eval suite. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-model quantization profiles with measured ROUGE/QA deltas.
[04:32] Sam O'Donnell: can we run a quick AB with q8 and the base fp16 model in a canary?
[04:36] Avery Chen: yes, we usually do a canary on a small percentage of traffic with evaluation callbacks. we'll set up an A/B fixed-sample evaluation so you can inspect for clinical-grade regressions.
[04:46] Lena Morris: about throughput guarantees: how does Redwood guarantee throughput in Reserved capacity? is bursting allowed?
[04:51] Marco Alvarez: Reserved (Dedicated) capacity is pooled — you commit to a certain GPU count and throughput. we offer burst credits for short spikes depending on available headroom in the same region. we also support autoscale policies for Dedicated with lead time and cooldown windows, but those are contractual for enterprise.
[05:08] Doug Patel: what's the SLA remediation if you miss latency SLOs?
[05:11] Avery Chen: remediation depends on plan — Enterprise Dedicated SLAs include credits tied to uptime and latency buckets. we'll share the exact SLO language.
[05:17] Rachel Kim: on VPC/private deployment — if we want control plane on our VPC with private data plane, is that supported?
[05:23] Priya Singh: yes, Private mode supports a customer-managed control plane or a hybrid with a managed control plane and customer data plane. we can run the data plane on-prem or in your VPC, integrate with HSM/KMS, and export audit logs to your SIEM.
[05:36] Sam O'Donnell: how invasive is the on-prem footprint? we don't want a huge ops burden.
[05:40] Priya Singh: the package is designed to be lightweight containers with automated upgrades via your internal airgap channel. we provide deployment templates and runbooks. the biggest ops work is GPU provisioning and networking; otherwise the runtime handles model lifecycle.
[05:51] Avery Chen: let's talk about routing and fallback policies — in hosted we often use model-variant fallback (smaller quantized model) when latency spikes, but that can affect quality. in Dedicated you can route to a reserved pool first and only fallback to hosted variants as a last resort.
[06:08] Lena Morris: can we define a policy: prefer Dedicated pool for p95-critical routes, but allow hosted fallback with reduced context to keep availability?
[06:14] Marco Alvarez: yes, routing policy supports hierarchical fallbacks: first try Dedicated with full context, then fallback to Dedicated with reduced context (KV eviction), then fallback to hosted quantized variant, then finally to a synchronous degraded response with a retry link.
[06:27] Doug Patel: how quickly does routing switch? in our payments batch windows we need sub-second failovers.
[06:33] Marco Alvarez: routing decisions are near-real-time — detection + change typically in hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds depending on propagation. for sub-second failover we recommend sticky proxy approaches at the customer side or pre-warmed cold spares.
[06:45] Sam O'Donnell: what telemetry do you expose for these decisions?
[06:49] Priya Singh: we expose per-request traces, token-level latency breakdowns, queue lengths, and KV hit ratios. you can plug those into your observability stack or use Redwood Console.
[06:58] Rachel Kim: are logs PII filtered before leaving our VPC in hybrid?
[07:02] Avery Chen: yes, we have configurable redaction rules and retention policies; also we can keep traces entirely in your VPC for Private mode.
[07:10] Lena Morris: ok let's talk pilot scope — what do you recommend?
[07:14] Marco Alvarez: pilot proposal: 2-week benchmarking on a representative sample — 1) Hosted baseline with normal routing, 2) Hosted with prefetch and stricter batching windows, 3) Dedicated small pool with tenant fencing, 4) Dedicated with autoscale enabled. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, KV hit ratios, and cost per 1M tokens.
[07:35] Doug Patel: do you have a concise config checklist we can review?
[07:38] Priya Singh: yes, we'll share a playbook with params: batch window ms, max batch size, kv ttl, kv cap per-tenant, quantization profile, fallback chain, routing priority.
[07:48] Sam O'Donnell: and we'll provide live traces and sample payloads — maybe about 5000 requests covering the worst-case long context flows.
[07:55] Avery Chen: great — next steps captured. any final security questions?
[07:58] Rachel Kim: one last— data residency. can we ensure all inference logs stay in eu-west-1?
[08:03] Priya Singh: yes, region pinning is supported for both Hosted (tenant regioning) and Dedicated deployments; Private obviously fully under your control.
[08:11] Lena Morris: awesome. thanks everyone.
[08:14] Avery Chen: thanks, we'll send the SLA playbook and cost model.
[08:17] (crosstalk)
